paragraphs: 16 When Joseph saw Benjamin with his brothers, he said to the steward of his house, “Take these men to my house. Slaughter an animal and prepare it, for they shall dine with me at noon.” 17 The man did as Joseph had commanded and took the brothers to Joseph’s house.

18 But the brothers were frightened that they had been taken to Joseph’s house. “We have been brought here because of the silver that was returned in our bags the first time,” they said. “They intend to overpower us and take us as slaves, along with our donkeys.”

19 So they approached Joseph’s steward and spoke to him at the entrance to the house. 20 “Please, sir,” they said, “we really did come down here the first time to buy food. 21 But when we came to the place we lodged for the night, we opened our sacks and, behold, each of us found his silver in the mouth of his sack! It was the full amount of our silver, and we have brought it back with us. 22 We have brought additional silver with us to buy food. We do not know who put our silver in our sacks.”

23 “It is fine,” said the steward. “Do not be afraid. Your God, the God of your father, gave you the treasure that was in your sacks. I received your silver.” Then he brought Simeon out to them. 24 And the steward took the men into Joseph’s house, gave them water to wash their feet, and provided food for their donkeys.

25 Since the brothers had been told that they were going to eat a meal there, they prepared their gift for Joseph’s arrival at noon. 26 When Joseph came home, they presented him with the gifts they had brought, and they bowed to the ground before him.
27 He asked if they were well, and then he asked, “How is your elderly father you told me about? Is he still alive?”
28 “Your servant our father is well,” they answered. “He is still alive.” And they bowed down to honor him.

29 When Joseph looked up and saw his brother Benjamin, his own mother’s son, he asked, “Is this your youngest brother, the one you told me about?” Then he declared, “May God be gracious to you, my son.”

30 Joseph hurried out because he was moved to tears for his brother, and he went to a private room to weep. 31 Then he washed his face and came back out. Regaining his composure, he said, “Serve the meal.”

32 They separately served Joseph, his brothers, and the Egyptians. They ate separately because the Egyptians would not eat with the Hebrews, since that was detestable to them. 33 They were seated before Joseph in order by age, from the firstborn to the youngest, and the men looked at one another in astonishment. 34 When the portions were served to them from Joseph’s table, Benjamin’s portion was five times larger than any of the others. So they feasted and drank freely with Joseph.

context_lines: When Joseph sees Benjamin, he tells his steward to bring the men home and prepare a meal. The brothers interpret the invitation as a threat, fearing that the returned silver will be used as a reason to enslave them. At the entrance they explain what happened and offer the money back, together with payment for more grain.

The steward reassures them, says that their God and their father's God gave them the treasure, and confirms that he received their silver. He brings Simeon out to them. Water is provided for washing their feet, and their donkeys are fed. The reception they feared becomes an unexpected welcome.

The reassurance begins with שָׁלוֹם, *šālôm* (shah-LOHM), peace or well-being. [Brown–Driver–Briggs](https://biblehub.com/hebrew/7965.htm) specifically records this reassuring use in Genesis 43:23. It answers their immediate fear and is followed by actions that give them reason to relax.

When Joseph arrives, the brothers present their gifts and bow before him. He asks about their father's welfare and blesses Benjamin. Seeing his full brother moves him so deeply that he leaves to weep privately, then washes his face and returns to the meal.

Joseph, the brothers, and the Egyptians are served separately; the account explains that the Egyptians regard eating with Hebrews as detestable. The brothers are astonished to find themselves seated in birth order. Benjamin receives five times the portion of the others, yet they feast and drink freely with Joseph. The scene leaves them together in hospitality before the more searching test of the next chapter.
common_interpretation_lines: Christians commonly see a welcome that exceeds the brothers' frightened expectations, along with Joseph's affection and the continuing movement toward reunion. [Wesley's notes on Genesis 43:23, 26, 29, 33–34](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-first-book-of-moses-called-genesis/) emphasize the steward's reassurance, the renewed bowing, Joseph's prayer for Benjamin, and the brothers' astonishment and relief.
current_position_lines: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.
god_plan_lines: Kindness now joins the pressure that has brought the brothers back. They have spoken of their guilt and fear punishment, yet receive food, reassurance, their brother Simeon, and a place at the table. Joseph's hidden identity does not prevent his care from reaching them.

This offers a clear connection with the wider theme in [Romans 2:4](https://biblehub.com/bsb/romans/2.htm): God's kindness leads people toward repentance. Joseph's welcome does not erase the past or finish the reconciliation in this chapter. It shows how generosity can open a way forward as the family's response continues to unfold.
